Family Health

Winter skin care: protect the barrier before adding more products

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Cold outdoor air and dry indoor heat can leave skin tight, flaky or irritated. The answer does not have to be a monthly facial or a complicated collection of serums. A routine that reduces irritation and helps retain moisture is often a more useful place to start.

Change the routine when the skin changes

Products that felt comfortable in warmer weather may sting or feel insufficient when the air becomes drier. Notice whether the problem is tightness, flaking, itch, redness or cracking rather than treating every change as a need for exfoliation.

Wash gently with a fragrance-free cleanser and use warm rather than very hot water. Avoid prolonged hot showers and vigorous rubbing. After washing, pat the skin and apply moisturizer while it is still slightly damp.

Choose moisture that suits your skin

Creams or ointments may protect very dry areas better than a light lotion. The best option is one you tolerate and can use consistently. A richer product for the hands does not have to be the same product used on an acne-prone face.

Ingredients such as glycerin, ceramides or hyaluronic acid may help support hydration. Hyaluronic acid is a moisturizing ingredient, not an exfoliating acid. A high concentration or a long ingredient list is not automatically better.

A moisturizer can temporarily soften the appearance of dryness-related lines, but it does not permanently erase wrinkles or reverse all sun damage. If a product burns or causes a persistent rash, stop using it and seek advice rather than assuming the sensation proves it is working.

Be cautious with peels and scrubs

Dry flakes are not an invitation to scrub harder. Strong exfoliants and frequent acid treatments can worsen irritation, particularly when the skin is already inflamed or cracked. Let comfortable basic care take priority.

A professional peel may have a role for a particular skin concern, but winter does not automatically make it suitable or safe. Discuss your skin condition, current medicines and any pregnancy or breastfeeding with a qualified clinician before choosing an active treatment.

Do not combine several new exfoliating products at once. A clinician can help adjust acne or other prescribed treatments if winter dryness makes them difficult to tolerate, rather than having you abandon needed treatment or add an aggressive facial.

Glycolic acid peels and salicylic acid treatments are examples sometimes offered for dullness, pigment concerns or acne. Their suitability depends on concentration, skin condition and the treatment plan; a cold season does not remove irritation or sun-sensitivity risks.

The idea that everyone’s skin-cell turnover slows in winter is too simple to guide treatment. A hydrating mask may be comfortable if well tolerated, but neither masks nor monthly facials are necessary to restore circulation or rebuild the skin.

Keep protection in the routine

Sun exposure still matters in winter. Use shade, protective clothing and broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher on exposed skin. Cold weather or a cloudy sky does not remove the need for sun protection.

Protect hands from cold air and wet work, and reapply moisturizer after washing. A simple lip balm or petrolatum can help dry lips. Soft fabrics may be more comfortable against irritated skin.

A humidifier may help in a dry room if it is maintained and cleaned according to its instructions. Drinking normally supports general health, but drinking excessive water is not a substitute for protecting the skin’s outer barrier.

Treat product claims as optional, not essential

Antioxidant and growth-factor products are marketed with promises about repair, firmness and cell renewal. Their effects depend on the formulation and evidence for the specific product. They are not essential purchases for ordinary winter dryness.

If you enjoy a facial, tell the practitioner about sensitive areas and everything you already apply. Avoid a treatment that leaves the skin raw or persistently painful. A relaxing experience and a proven medical treatment are different claims.

See a clinician if dryness persists despite gentle care, becomes painful or bleeds, or comes with a spreading or recurrent rash. Eczema, contact allergy and other conditions can need targeted treatment rather than another cosmetic product.

Growth factors are signalling molecules involved in biological processes such as repair. That role does not prove that a cosmetic serum delivers clinically meaningful collagen production, firmness or rejuvenation. Similarly, antioxidant activity in a laboratory is not a promise to reverse accumulated pollution or sun damage.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Prioritize comfortable cleansing, regular moisturizer and protection of the skin barrier.

Peels, masks, antioxidants and growth-factor products are optional and need product-specific evidence rather than seasonal promises.

How BeMama can help

Tell the clinician or practitioner what you already use and simplify the routine if products sting or worsen dryness.

When to seek help

Pain, bleeding, persistent rash or spreading inflammation deserves clinical review rather than stronger exfoliation.

Sources and further reading

  • American Academy of Dermatology — Dermatologists’ top tips for relieving dry skin
  • American Academy of Dermatology — Cold weather and your skin

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Start with gentle cleansing and regular moisturizer.
  • Do not scrub or peel already irritated skin to remove flakes.
  • Keep winter sun protection and seek help for persistent or painful changes.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a professional facial every month in winter?

No. Many people manage dryness with a simple home routine. Professional treatment should address a specific need and suit the skin.

Does hyaluronic acid exfoliate the skin?

No. It is used for hydration. The word acid does not mean every ingredient acts like a peeling treatment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
